app.name: Latin Beat Machine
app.description: An interactive Salsa & Bachata rhythm trainer. Build your own beat from real percussion, practice at your own tempo, and train your ear.

salsa.name: Salsa
salsa.title: Salsa Rhythm Trainer
salsa.description: Build a Salsa rhythm from clave, congas, bongos, timbales, cowbell, maracas and güiro, then practice it at your own tempo.

bachata.name: Bachata
bachata.title: Bachata Rhythm Trainer
bachata.description: Build a Bachata rhythm from güira, bongos, campana, bass, requinto and segunda, then practice it at your own tempo.

presets.salsa-son-2-3: Son montuno — where salsa comes from

presets.salsa-verse-3-2: The steady groove under the singing. Clear clave and congas: the best place to start.
presets.salsa-montuno-3-2: The hotter part after the verse: the bongo and timbales bells come in and the band pushes forward.
presets.salsa-mambo-3-2: The instrumental peak: the singers step back and the brass plays the mambo. The trombones keep a riff going, the trumpets punch out the clave over it — the dancers' cue for shines.
presets.bachata-derecho: The calm groove of the verse. Good for practising basic steps.
presets.bachata-majao: The chorus: the bongos and güira drop the offbeats and land on each count.
presets.bachata-mambo: The climax: the bell rings on every count, the dancers' cue for footwork.
presets.salsa-verse-2-3: The same verse, but the clave starts from its "2" side. Compare it with 3-2 to hear where a phrase begins.
presets.salsa-montuno-2-3: The montuno with the clave started from its "2" side.
presets.salsa-mambo-2-3: The mambo with the clave started from its "2" side.
presets.salsa-chachacha-2-3: Around 120 BPM. Listen to the güiro: two short scrapes and a long one are the "cha-cha-chá" you step on 4 & 1.
presets.salsa-guaguanco-3-2: The street rumba salsa bands quote in "rumba" breaks. Rumba clave: the third stroke comes half a beat later than in son clave. Simplified for one conga player.
presets.salsa-on2-3-2: For dancing "on 2": the voice counts only 2 and 6, where you break, and the congas lead — their slap lands on the same counts.
presets.salsa-son-2-3: Slower Cuban son, as a septeto plays it: bongó, maracas, tres and bass, no congas or piano. Good for hearing the clave and tres clearly.
presets.salsa-bolero: Around 80 BPM, each count a real beat. Soft maracas and bongó, bass on 1 and 3: for slow, close dancing.
presets.salsa-pachanga-2-3: Early-1960s charanga craze, between cha-cha-chá and salsa in tempo. The congas slap on the beat and bounce with two open tones after it.
presets.song: A song you put together from the presets below. Change its sections in the song panel; Reset throws away grid edits.
presets.custom: Someone shared this pattern with you. Edit it freely; Reset goes back to the first preset.

instruments.voice: A voice counting the dance: 1 to 8. Use it to find the 1.
instruments.clave: Two wooden sticks. Their pattern (3-2) is the backbone the whole salsa band follows.
instruments.congas: Tall hand drums. Heel and toe rock quietly on the drum; the open tones on 4 and 4& are the heartbeat of salsa (the tumbao).
instruments.bongos: Two small joined drums. Steady eighth notes that keep the band moving.
instruments.timbales: Two metal drums played with sticks. On the shell they play the cáscara pattern.
instruments.cowbell: The bongo player's hand bell (campana). In the montuno it replaces the bongos: the mouth on the beat, the neck in between.
instruments.timbalebell: The bell mounted on the timbales: the mambo bell in the montuno, the cha-cha bell in cha-cha-chá. Higher than the bongo bell.
instruments.maracas: Shakers. A soft, even pulse on every eighth note.
instruments.guiro: A ridged gourd scraped with a stick: long and short scrapes.
instruments.guira: A metal scraper, the sound you hear through the whole bachata: long on the beat, short in between.
instruments.campana: A bell the bongo player switches to in the mambo. When you hear it, the mambo has started.
instruments.bass: Plays the low notes of the chords. In bachata it marks the 1; in salsa it plays the next chord early, on 4, and skips the 1 (the tumbao).
instruments.piano: The montuno: a repeating, syncopated piano figure locked to the clave. "push" plays the next chord ahead of the bar.
instruments.tres: The Cuban tres: three pairs of strings struck with a pick. It plays the guajeo, a repeating figure locked to the clave. Played here from guitar recordings.
instruments.trumpet: The trumpets: in the montuno they play the moña, a short riff that ends by pushing the next chord early. "hit" is a short stab on the whole chord.
instruments.trombone: The trombones: lower and darker than the trumpets. In the montuno they answer the trumpets’ riff with stabs on the other side of the clave.
instruments.requinto: The lead guitar: high melodies and runs between the singer's lines.
instruments.segunda: The rhythm guitar: plays the chords in a steady, rolling pattern.

controls.speed: How fast the music plays. Normal is the usual tempo for this rhythm; start slow while learning.
controls.voice: A voice counting along: just the numbers, or with “and” between them.
controls.counts: How many counts the loop lasts before it repeats. Dancers count in blocks of 8.
controls.chords: The chord for each bar. The bass, guitars and piano follow it.
controls.random: Fills the grid with random hits. Fun for experimenting.
controls.clear: Removes every hit, so you can build a rhythm from scratch.
controls.advancedMode: Loop length, chords and the volumes beside the grid.
controls.simpleMode: Hide the extra controls. Your rhythm and settings stay as they are.
controls.count: The count the music is on right now. 1 and 5 start each half of the 8 counts: listen for them.
controls.share: A link to this exact pattern — tempo, length, mutes and all. On a phone it opens the share menu, on a computer it copies the link. Send it to a partner or your students.
controls.reset: Throws away your changes and goes back to the preset.
controls.stepper: Tap for 1 BPM, hold to change by 5.
controls.animation: Icons and counts move in time with the music. Switch it off if it distracts you.

mix.label: Listen
mix.hint: On its own: just this instrument. With the band: everyone, a little quieter, so the instrument stands out.

congas.title: Congas in salsa: the tumbao
congas.description: How the congas sound in salsa: the heel, toe, slap and open strokes, the tumbao rhythm, and where a dancer finds the count in it. Listen on its own and with the band.
congas.about:
Congas (tumbadoras) are tall Cuban drums with a skin head, played with the hands. A conguero usually has two or three drums of different sizes in front of them, sitting or standing between them.
In salsa the congas play the tumbao: a short figure, one bar long, repeated through the whole song. It is the band's pulse: other instruments change parts, the tumbao stays.
congas.strokes:
Heel and toe: the hand rocks on the head, first the base of the palm, then the fingers. They're quiet, nearly lost in the band, but they keep the hand moving and the eighth notes even.
Slap: a sharp, cracking stroke with the fingers near the rim, on 2 (and 6).
Open: the fingers strike near the rim and bounce straight off, so the head rings out as a note. The two open tones on 4 and & (8 and &) are the tumbao's "boom-boom".
congas.dancer:
The two open tones tell you where you are in the bar: right after them comes 1 or 5. Lost the count? Find that "boom-boom" in the music and come in on the next beat.
The slap on 2 and 6 suits those who dance On2: their break, the change of direction, lands on it.

tumbao.name: Full
tumbao.description: The full tumbao: heel and toe on 1 and 3, the slap on 2, open tones on 4 and &.

slap-open.name: Slap
slap-open.description: Heel and toe left out: the slap on 2 and the open tones on 4 and &. The second step in learning the tumbao.

open.name: Open
open.description: Only the open tones on 4 and & — what a dancer hears best in the band. Learning the tumbao starts here.

clave.title: Clave in salsa: 3-2, 2-3 and rumba clave
clave.description: What the clave is in salsa: two sticks, and the five-stroke rhythm the band is built on. Listen to son clave 3-2 and 2-3 and rumba clave, on its own and with the band.
clave.about:
Claves are two sticks of hard wood. One rests on a cupped palm, which works as a resonator, and the other strikes it. The sound is dry and high, and cuts through the whole band.
The rhythm played on them has the same name: five strokes over two bars. All of salsa is built on it: piano, bells and horns are written "in clave", so their parts fit it.
clave.strokes:
There's one stroke: stick on stick. What matters is not how but when: three strokes in one bar, two in the other.
In 3-2 the three come first (1, the & of 2, 4), then the two (6 and 7). In 2-3 it's the same figure started from its second bar: two, then three.
Rumba clave differs by one stroke: the third stroke of the three-side moves from 4 to the & of 4. The rhythm pulls more — it's what rumba guaguancó is played in.
clave.dancer:
In a song you often can't hear the clave, but the whole band holds on to it. The strokes on 6 and 7 in 3-2 land with the steps of the basic's second half — a good landmark.
If the band's accents don't seem to fit the count, listen for where the clave has three strokes and where two: 3-2 and 2-3 sound different, though the dancer's count stays the same.

son-3-2.description: Son clave 3-2: 1, & of 2, 4 — 6, 7. Over the 3-2 verse.

son-2-3.description: Son clave 2-3: 2, 3 — 5, & of 6, 8. Over the 2-3 verse.

rumba-3-2.name: Rumba
rumba-3-2.description: Rumba clave 3-2: the third stroke on the & of 4 instead of 4. Over the guaguancó.

bongos.title: Bongos in salsa: the martillo
bongos.description: How the bongos sound in salsa: the macho and the hembra, the martillo rhythm, and what it tells a dancer. Listen on its own and with the band, in the verse and in a slow bolero.
bongos.about:
Bongos are two small drums joined together: the small macho and the larger hembra. The bongocero holds them between the knees and plays with the fingers.
In the verse the bongos play the martillo; in the montuno the bongocero puts them down and picks up a hand bell, the bongo bell.
bongos.strokes:
High: strokes on the macho, bright and ringing. Low: an open stroke on the hembra, deeper. Slap: a sharp accent the bongocero decorates with.
The martillo ("hammer"): even eighth notes on the macho, an open stroke on the hembra on 4, and a rest on the & of 4. On real bongos the macho strokes alternate fingers and thumb, which gives the "ta-ka-ta-ka".
bongos.dancer:
The martillo is the steadiest part in the verse: the busy macho strokes set the tempo, and the low stroke on 4 and 8, like the congas' open tones, marks the end of the bar just before 1 and 5.
The rest on the & of 4 and 8 is a breath before the new bar: the step starts right after it.

martillo.name: Verse
martillo.description: The martillo in the salsa verse, 3-2.

bolero.name: Bolero
bolero.description: The same martillo in a bolero — slow, about 80 counts a minute: easy to make out every stroke.

cowbell.title: The bongo bell in salsa: the campana
cowbell.description: The bongocero's hand bell (campana): how it's played in the salsa montuno, and why it's the easiest thing to keep the count by. Listen on its own and with the band.
cowbell.about:
The campana is a hand bell the bongocero switches to in the montuno, the most energetic part of a song. It's held in one hand and struck with a stick.
When it comes in, the music gets louder and denser: that's the sign the montuno has started.
cowbell.strokes:
Mouth: a stroke on the wide end, loud and open. Neck: a stroke near the narrow end, short and dull.
The rhythm is simple: the mouth on 1 and 3 (5 and 7), the neck on 2 and 4 (6 and 8) — a stroke on every count.
cowbell.dancer:
The bongo bell strikes evenly on every count — the clearest metronome in the band. The loud mouth strokes fall on 1, 3, 5 and 7.
Lost? Hold on to the bell: "1" is a loud stroke followed by a quiet one.

bongo-bell.name: Montuno
bongo-bell.description: The bongo bell in the montuno: the mouth on 1 and 3, the neck on 2 and 4.

timbalebell.title: The timbales bell in salsa: the mambo bell
timbalebell.description: The timbales bell (mambo bell): how its pattern follows the 3-2 and 2-3 clave, and how it changes in cha-cha-chá. Listen on its own and with the band.
timbalebell.about:
A bell mounted on the timbales stand. In the verse the timbalero plays cáscara on the drum's shell; in the montuno and the mambo they move to the bell.
It's higher and sharper than the bongo bell, and in the montuno the two play together.
timbalebell.strokes:
Mouth: an open stroke, on every count. Neck: quiet strokes in between, where the cáscara's strokes are. That's why the mambo bell keeps the clave's shape, and differs in 3-2 and 2-3.
In cha-cha-chá the bell is simpler: only open strokes, one on every count.
timbalebell.dancer:
The open strokes on every count keep the pulse; the quiet neck strokes tell you which half of the clave you're in.
In cha-cha-chá the bell strikes every count — easy to keep a slow tempo by.

mambo-3-2.description: The mambo bell in the montuno, 3-2 clave.

mambo-2-3.description: The mambo bell in the montuno, 2-3 clave: the same pattern started from its second bar.

chachacha.name: Cha-cha-chá
chachacha.description: The bell in cha-cha-chá: an open stroke on every count.

guiro.title: The güiro in salsa
guiro.description: The güiro in salsa and cha-cha-chá: how its long and short scrapes are played, and where they meet a dancer's steps. Listen on its own and with the band.
guiro.about:
The güiro is a hollow gourd with notches cut in it (today often wood or plastic). A stick scraped along the notches gives a rasping sound.
It came to salsa from Cuban son and danzón, and is heard best in cha-cha-chá and the montuno.
guiro.strokes:
Long: the stick runs along all the notches, and the sound draws out. Short: a quick, short scrape.
The pattern takes two counts: a long scrape on 1, two short ones on 2 and its &. Then the same on 3 and 4.
guiro.dancer:
The long scrape draws out from an odd count to the even one; the short "ch-ch" falls on 2 and &, 4 and &.
In cha-cha-chá the short ones on 4 and & land right on the dancer's "cha-cha".

montuno.name: Montuno
montuno.description: The güiro in the salsa montuno, along with the bells.

chachacha.name: Cha-cha-chá
chachacha.description: The same pattern in cha-cha-chá — slower, about 120 counts a minute.

timbales.title: Timbales in salsa: the cáscara
timbales.description: How the timbales sound in salsa: the cáscara on the shell, strokes on the heads and the timbalero's fills. Listen to cáscara in 3-2 and 2-3 and the cha-cha-chá rhythm, on its own and with the band.
timbales.about:
Timbales are two metal drums on a stand — the higher macho and the lower hembra — with bells and sometimes a cymbal. The timbalero plays with sticks.
They came from Cuban danzón and charanga. In a salsa band the timbalero leads the moves from one part of a song to the next.
timbales.strokes:
Rim: the stick on the drum's metal shell, a dry click. It's what the cáscara is played on.
High and low: strokes on the macho and hembra heads, for accents and fills — short rolls before a new part of the song.
The cáscara follows the clave, so it differs in 3-2 and 2-3. In cha-cha-chá it's simpler: a click on the shell on 2 and an open hembra on 4.
timbales.dancer:
The cáscara is dense and steady through the verse. What helps a dancer most are the timbalero's fills: a short roll at the end of an eight warns that a new part of the song is coming.
In cha-cha-chá the open stroke on 4 is the cue for the "cha-cha".

cascara-2-3.description: Cáscara in the verse, 2-3 clave: the same pattern started from its second bar.

chachacha.name: Cha-cha-chá
chachacha.description: Cha-cha-chá: a click on the shell on 2, the open hembra on 4.

maracas.title: Maracas in salsa
maracas.description: Maracas in salsa and son: how they sound, and why they help you feel the & between the counts. Listen on its own and with the band.
maracas.about:
Maracas are a pair of rattles on handles: hollow shells (once gourds) with seeds or shot inside.
They're among the oldest instruments of son. In salsa they're often played by one of the singers in the chorus.
maracas.strokes:
There's one sound: a short "sh" from a sharp flick of the wrist, as the seeds hit the shell.
The hands alternate, so the maracas sound evenly on every eighth note.
maracas.dancer: Even eighths are the grid everything else sits on. When the count is hard to hear, the maracas help you feel the & between counts and keep your steps even.

eighths.name: Verse
eighths.description: Eighth notes in the salsa verse.

son.name: Son
son.description: In son — slower, about 110 counts a minute, with the bongos and the tres.

bass.title: Bass in salsa: the tumbao
bass.description: How the bass plays in salsa: the bass tumbao, the push on 4, and why the bass almost never plays the 1. Listen on its own and with the band, in salsa and cha-cha-chá.
bass.about: The bass in salsa is an upright bass, a bass guitar or a "baby bass" (an electric upright). It carries the harmony with the piano and holds the rhythm with the congas.
bass.strokes:
The bass plays the root and fifth of the chord.
The bass tumbao: the fifth on the & of 2, then on 4 the next chord's root, held over the bar line. That's why the salsa bass almost never plays the 1.
In cha-cha-chá, pachanga and bolero the bass is simpler: the root on 1, the fifth on 3.
bass.dancer:
A bass that skips the 1 throws beginners off: the lowest note lands on 4 and rings into the 1. Don't look for the 1 in the bass — it's right after the long note on 4 (and 8).
In cha-cha-chá it's the other way round: the steady bass on 1 and 3 is a great landmark.

tumbao.name: Tumbao
tumbao.description: The bass tumbao in the verse: the fifth on the & of 2, the next root on 4.

one-three.name: On 1 and 3
one-three.description: The root on 1, the fifth on 3 — as in cha-cha-chá.

piano.title: Piano in salsa: the montuno
piano.description: How the piano plays in salsa: the montuno in 3-2 and 2-3 clave, the push on the & of 4, and bolero chords. Listen on its own and with the band.
piano.about: The piano in salsa plays the montuno: a repeating figure of chords and octaves, written to fit the clave. With the bass it sets the song's harmony.
piano.strokes:
Chord: several notes at once, short. Octave: one note of the chord in both hands, an octave apart.
Push: the next chord played on the & of 4, before the bar begins, and left ringing over the 1.
The 3-2 and 2-3 montunos are one pattern started from different bars. In a bolero the piano plays the chord on 1 and again on the & of 2.
piano.dancer: The montuno goes round and round through the whole song — the most recognizable part of the rhythm section. The push on the & of 4 (with the bass) makes the 1 feel like it has already arrived, so the step on 1 in salsa sounds like landing after a pickup.

montuno-3-2.description: The montuno in the verse, 3-2 clave.

montuno-2-3.description: The montuno in the verse, 2-3 clave.

bolero.name: Bolero
bolero.description: Bolero: the chord on 1 and on the & of 2.

tres.title: Tres in salsa: the guajeo
tres.description: The tres is the Cuban guitar with three double strings: how its guajeo sounds in salsa and in son. Listen on its own and with the band.
tres.about: The tres is a Cuban guitar with three pairs of strings, hence the name. It's the lead instrument of son, the music salsa grew out of. A salsa band doesn't always have one, but its metallic ring is easy to recognize.
tres.strokes:
The tres plays single chord notes and dyads — two notes together.
The guajeo is a pattern that fills the gaps the piano leaves. It has the same push on the & of 4, and no stroke on the 1 after it.
tres.dancer: When the piano and the tres play together, their parts mesh like gears. For a dancer the tres is the sound of old-school, son-flavored salsa; in son it leads the whole band.

guajeo-3-2.name: Verse
guajeo-3-2.description: The guajeo in the salsa verse, 3-2 clave.

son.name: Son
son.description: The guajeo in son, 2-3 clave: here the tres leads the band.

trumpet.title: Trumpets in salsa: moña and mambo
trumpet.description: How the trumpets play in salsa: the call and response with the trombones in the moña, and the clave in the mambo. Listen on its own and with the band.
trumpet.about: Trumpets are the top voice of a salsa band's horn section, usually two or three. They don't play the whole song, only certain parts: the moña in the montuno and the arranged mambo.
trumpet.strokes: The trumpets play chord notes (root, third, fifth), short hits as a section, and the push — a chord on the & of 4 that pulls into the next bar.
trumpet.dancer:
The trumpets coming in signal that the song has moved to a new part. In the moña the trumpets and trombones trade phrases: the trumpets call in the first bar, the trombones answer in the second.
In the mambo the trumpets punch out the clave rhythm — a good moment for accents in the dance.

mona.name: Moña
mona.description: The moña in the montuno: trumpets call, trombones answer.

mambo.name: Mambo
mambo.description: The mambo: the trumpets punch out the clave over the trombones' riff.

trombone.title: Trombones in salsa: moña and mambo
trombone.description: How the trombones play in salsa: answering the trumpets in the moña, and the riff in the mambo. Listen on its own and with the band.
trombone.about: Trombones are the low voice of the horn section. They gave 1960s–70s New York salsa its heavy, dense sound: Eddie Palmieri's and Willie Colón's bands were built on them.
trombone.strokes: The trombones play chord notes, short hits as a section, and the push — a chord on the & of 4 that pulls into the next bar.
trombone.dancer: In the moña the trombones answer the trumpets in the second bar. In the mambo they play a riff through both bars, pushing on the & of 4, while the trumpets punch out the clave over it.

mona.name: Moña
mona.description: The moña: the trombones answer the trumpets in the second bar.

mambo.name: Mambo
mambo.description: The mambo: a riff through both bars, under the trumpets.

guira.title: The güira in bachata
guira.description: The güira, a metal scraper, is bachata's metronome: how it sounds in the derecho, majao and mambo. Listen on its own and with the band.
guira.about: The güira is a metal cylinder punched with bumps, scraped with a metal brush. It's the Dominican cousin of the güiro. In bachata and merengue it keeps time, like a hi-hat in pop music.
guira.strokes:
Short: a quick, short scrape. Long: a scrape along the whole length.
In the derecho (verse) the güira plays even short scrapes on every eighth; in the majao (chorus), long ones on every count; in the mambo, a strict pattern: 1, the & of 2, 3, the & of 4.
guira.dancer: The güira is bachata's metronome. In the verse it ticks off eighths; in the chorus it moves to long scrapes on every count, and the music seems to open up. A change in the güira tells you the song has moved to another part.

derecho.name: Derecho
derecho.description: Derecho (verse): short scrapes on every eighth.

majao.name: Majao
majao.description: Majao (chorus): a long scrape on every count.

bongos.title: Bongos in bachata: martillo and majao
bongos.description: How the bongos sound in bachata: the martillo in the verse, strokes on the count in the chorus, and the low stroke on 4 that cues the tap. Listen on its own and with the band.
bongos.about: Bongos are two small drums joined together: the higher macho and the lower hembra. In bachata they're the main percussion: the bongocero drives the rhythm and decorates it.
bongos.strokes:
High: a stroke on the macho. Low: an open stroke on the hembra. Slap: a sharp accent.
In the derecho (verse) the bongos play the martillo: every eighth on the macho, the hembra on 4. In the majao (chorus) they drop the upbeats: macho on 1, 2, 3 and hembra on 4.
bongos.dancer: The low hembra stroke on 4 and 8 is the main landmark in bachata: it's where the tap of the basic step falls. Lost? Wait for that stroke and start on 1 right after it.

derecho.name: Derecho
derecho.description: Derecho (verse): the martillo, the hembra on 4.

majao.name: Majao
majao.description: Majao (chorus): only the counts, the hembra on 4.

campana.title: The campana in bachata
campana.description: The campana is the bongocero's hand bell in the bachata mambo: how it sounds and how to keep the count by it. Listen on its own and with the band.
campana.about: The campana is a hand bell. The bongocero picks it up in the mambo — the song's instrumental climax, when the singer stops and the requinto solos.
campana.strokes:
Mouth: a loud, open stroke. Neck: a short, dull one.
The mouth on 1 and 3, the neck on 2 and 4 — a stroke on every count.
campana.dancer: The bell comes in at the song's most energetic part. It's easy to keep the count by: loud strokes on 1 and 3 (5 and 7), quiet ones on 2 and 4.

mambo.name: Mambo
mambo.description: Mambo: the mouth on 1 and 3, the neck on 2 and 4.

bass.title: Bass in bachata
bass.description: How the bass plays in bachata: the root on 1 and 3, a pickup on the & of 2 and a note on 4. Listen on its own and with the band.
bass.about: The bass guitar in bachata sets the harmony and the bottom of the rhythm, together with the segunda.
bass.strokes: The bass plays the root and fifth of the chord: the root on 1 and 3, the fifth on the & of 2 and on 4. The first note rings for a count and a half.
bass.dancer: Unlike in salsa, the bachata bass plays the 1 — you hear it straight away. The note on 4, with the bongos' hembra, underlines the tap.

derecho.name: Derecho
derecho.description: The root on 1 and 3, the fifth on the & of 2 and on 4.

requinto.title: The requinto in bachata
requinto.description: The requinto is bachata's lead guitar: arpeggios in the verse, answers to the singer in the chorus, and the riff in the mambo. Listen on its own and with the band.
requinto.about: The requinto is bachata's first, lead guitar: small and tuned high. It's the voice of bachata — you know the style from the requinto's first notes.
requinto.strokes:
The requinto plays single chord notes (root, third, fifth) and dyads.
In the derecho it plays the chord's arpeggio up and down in eighths; in the majao, short answers to the singer; in the mambo, a repeating riff: the requinto takes the solo.
requinto.dancer: The requinto is the melody you dance to musically: its phrases tell you where to accent or pause. In the mambo, when the singer stops, it leads — time for the most striking moves.

derecho.name: Derecho
derecho.description: Derecho: an arpeggio up and down, a note per eighth.

majao.name: Majao
majao.description: Majao: a dyad on 4, a run down on 7 and 8.

segunda.title: The segunda in bachata
segunda.description: The segunda is bachata's rhythm guitar: bass notes on 1, 3 and 4 and strums on the other eighths. Listen on its own and with the band.
segunda.about: The segunda is bachata's second, rhythm guitar. It plays the chords and holds the harmony together with the bass.
segunda.strokes: A bass note on 1, 3 and 4, following the bass guitar, and short strums on the chord on the other eighths.
segunda.dancer: The segunda sounds on every eighth and, like the güira, keeps an even grid. Its bass notes land with the steps on 1 and 3 and the tap on 4.

derecho.name: Derecho
derecho.description: Bass notes on 1, 3 and 4, strums on the other eighths.
